title: S.Dhanasekaran vs Selvaraj.D on 12 December, 2024
full_text: S.Dhanasekaran vs Selvaraj.D on 12 December, 2024 IN THE COURT OF METROPOLITAN MAGISTRATE EAST DISTRICT, KARKARDOOMA COURTS, DELHI. Presided by: Sh. Divyam Lila S. Dhanasekaran versus Selvaraj D. Ct. Case No. : 4816/2018 Jurisdiction : P.S New Ashok Nagar Unique ID/ CNR No. : DLET02­008622­2018 Sh. S. Dhanasekaran, S/o Sh. Sivasamy, R/o 15­ Name of the Complainant : B, MIG Flats, Pocket­5, Mayur Vihar, Phase­3, Delhi­110096. Sh. Selvaraj D., S/o Sh. Dharmalingam S., R/o Name of the Accused(s) : 112b/2d, V.K.S. Colony, A. San Bye Pump No. 2, Sector­49, NOIDA, UP Counsel for the Complainant : Sh. S. Muthu, Ld. Counsel. Counsel for the Accused : Ms. K. Chandra Gandhi, Ld. Counsel. Date of instituion of case : 15.11.2018 Date of Judgment : 12.12.2024 Final Order : Acquitted Offence under Section : Under Section 138 NI Act ­:JUDGMENT:­ 5 Introduction: This case arises out of a complaint filed by the complainant, S. Dhanasekaran, under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (hereinafter referred to as the " NI Act ") alleging dishonor of a Page no. 1 / 11 In the court of Sh. Divyam Lila, MM, East district, Karkardooma courts, Delhi. cheque issued by the accused, Selvaraj. The cheque was dishonored 10 on 26.09.2018 when presented to the bank for payment, on the ground of "insufficient funds." The complainant asserts that the cheque was issued by the accused in discharge of a legally enforceable debt of ₹10,00,000/­ towards a loan given by him to the accused. Hence the present case has been filed by the complainant under Section 138 NI 15 act to seek compensation from and punishment to the accused; as complainant claims that accused failed to pay the cheque amount after dishonour of the cheque. Brief Facts of the Case The complainant claims that in May 2016, the accused approached him for a loan 20 of ₹10,00,000/­, which the complainant provided in cash. The complainant asserts that the loan was given without any written agreement but was represented by the cheque bearing No. 136521 dated 28.08.2018, drawn by the accused on his bank account. According to the complainant, the cheque was dishonored when presented on 26.09.2018, due to insufficient funds in the accused's account. 25 In response to the dishonor, the complainant sent a legal notice to the accused on 12.10.2018 demanding payment, but the notice was returned unclaimed. Consequently, the complainant filed this complaint under Section 138 of the NI Act, seeking recovery of the loan amount along with interest and costs. On the other hand, the accused denies the entire transaction. He contends that the 30 CC no. 4816/2018 S. Dhanasekaran Vs. Selvaraj D. Page no. 2 / 11 In the court of Sh. Divyam Lila, MM, East district, Karkardooma courts, Delhi. cheque was issued in the context of a business partnership with the complainant's father and was not issued for any personal loan. According to the accused, several disputes arose between him and the complainant's father concerning their joint business, S.S. Auto Finance, and the cheque was part of business transactions that were misused by the complainant's father in furtherance of the disputes. The 35 accused also claims that the legal notice sent by the complainant was deliberately returned unclaimed, and the complainant is trying to misuse the situation. Brief of Evidence Evidence Led by the Complainant 1. Affidavit of the evidence of the Complainant (CW­1): The complainant 40 deposed that he gave a friendly loan of ₹10,00,000/­ to the accused in May 2016. He claimed that the loan was given in cash, without any formal documentation, and that the cheque in question was issued by the accused to repay the loan. 2. Cheque (Ex. CW­1/1): The complainant submitted the dishonored cheque, 45 No. 136521, dated 28.08.2018, as evidence. The cheque was returned unpaid due to "insufficient funds." 3. Cheque Return Memo (Ex. CW­1/2): The complainant presented the cheque return memo, which indicated the reason for dishonor as insufficient funds in the accused's account. 50 4. Legal Notice (Ex. CW­1/3): The complainant's lawyer sent a legal notice to CC no. 4816/2018 S. Dhanasekaran Vs. Selvaraj D. Page no. 3 / 11 In the court of Sh. Divyam Lila, MM, East district, Karkardooma courts, Delhi. the accused on 12.10.2018, demanding the repayment of the loan amount. This notice was returned unclaimed, which was submitted as Ex. CW­1/4. 5. Unclaimed Legal Notice (Ex. CW­1/4): The returned legal notice was submitted as evidence to show that the accused had deliberately refused to 55 accept the notice. Evidence Led by the Accused 1. Chief Examination of the Accused (DW­1): The accused deposed that the cheque was issued in connection with a business arrangement between him and the complainant's father. He stated that the cheque was part of several 60 transactions and disputes related to the partnership in S.S. Auto Finance, a business jointly run by him and the complainant's father. 2. Partnership Dispute Documents (Ex. CW­1/DX1): The accused produced documents related to ongoing litigation with the complainant's father, including a series of cases regarding business disputes. These cases were 65 filed in Coimbatore, Pollachi, and Mannarkkad. The accused contended that the cheque in question was issued as part of the business dealings, not as a personal loan. 3. Litigation Records (Ex. CW­1/DX2): The accused submitted copies of multiple litigation records between him and the complainant's father, 70 showing the business disputes and the role of the cheque in the larger context of their partnership disagreements. 4. Sale Deed (Ex. CW­1/DX3): The accused presented a sale deed executed in favor of the complainant's father to demonstrate a settlement between him CC no. 4816/2018 S. Dhanasekaran Vs. Selvaraj D. Page no. 4 / 11 In the court of Sh. Divyam Lila, MM, East district, Karkardooma courts, Delhi. 5 and the complainant's father concerning losses from their partnership. The 75 accused claimed that this document evidenced the repayment of business­ related financial obligations. Issues for consideration: The central issues in this case are as follows: 1. Whether the cheque was issued in discharge of a legally enforceable debt or liability? 80 2. Whether the accused successfully rebutted the presumption under Section 139 of the NI Act that the cheque was issued for a valid consideration? 3. Whether the complainant has discharged his burden of proving the existence of the loan and the debt? Presumption Under Section 139 of the NI Act 85 Section 139 of the NI Act raises a statutory presumption that a cheque is issued in discharge of a legally enforceable debt or liability. This presumption is a rebuttable one, which means that while the complainant may prove the dishonor of the cheque and the existence of the cheque transaction, the accused can lead evidence to rebut the presumption by showing that the cheque was not issued for a valid 90 debt. In this case, the complainant has provided sufficient evidence to establish the dishonor of the cheque (Ex. CW­1/1) and has submitted the cheque return memo CC no. 4816/2018 S. Dhanasekaran Vs. Selvaraj D. Page no. 5 / 11 In the court of Sh. Divyam Lila, MM, East district, Karkardooma courts, Delhi. (Ex. CW­1/2) from the bank, which indicates that the cheque was dishonored due to "Insufficient Funds" in the accused's account. This satisfies the requirement for 95 triggering the presumption under Section 138 of the NI Act. However, the presumption created by Section 139 is not conclusive. The accused has the opportunity to rebut this presumption by presenting evidence to show that the cheque was not issued for a legally enforceable debt. In the case at hand, the accused has done so by presenting a detailed defense regarding the context in 100 which the cheque was issued, supported by documentary evidence. Rebuttal of the Presumption: The Accused's Defense The accused has made several assertions and produced documentary evidence to challenge the complainant's claim. According to the accused, the cheque was issued in connection with a business partnership between him and the 105 complainant's father, and not as repayment for a loan. He has raised the defense of a business dispute between him and the complainant's father, which allegedly involved the issuance of the cheque as part of the settlement of financial obligations related to their business dealings. The accused has led the following evidence in his defense: 110 • Affidavit of the Accused (DW­1): The accused claims that the cheque was issued in the course of business dealings between him and the complainant's father and that it was not issued for a personal loan. He stated that the cheque was part of a broader series of transactions related to their joint CC no. 4816/2018 S. Dhanasekaran Vs. Selvaraj D. Page no. 6 / 11 In the court of Sh. Divyam Lila, MM, East district, Karkardooma courts, Delhi. business, S.S. Auto Finance, and was misused by the complainant in the 115 course of their ongoing partnership disputes. • Partnership Dispute Documents (Ex. CW­1/DX1): The accused produced documents of ongoing litigation between him and the complainant's father concerning disputes in their joint business venture. These documents indicate that there were multiple legal proceedings and unsettled financial 120 matters between the two parties, which could have given rise to the issuance of the cheque in question. • Sale Deed (Ex. CW­1/DX3): The accused submitted a sale deed executed by him in favor of the complainant's father, which he argued showed that certain financial obligations related to their business partnership had been 125 settled. This was further evidence to support his claim that the cheque was issued not as a personal loan repayment, but as part of the business arrangement. The accused's defense hinges on the argument that the cheque was issued in connection with a business dispute and not as part of a personal loan transaction. 130 He presented credible evidence in the form of litigation records and a sale deed that substantiate his claim of a business relationship and disputes involving the complainant's father. On the preponderance of probabilities, the court finds that the accused has raised a plausible defense. The documentary evidence presented by the accused, including 135 litigation records and the sale deed, paints a clear picture of an ongoing dispute regarding business matters. It is reasonable to infer that the cheque, which was CC no. 4816/2018 S. Dhanasekaran Vs. Selvaraj D. Page no. 7 / 11 In the court of Sh. Divyam Lila, MM, East district, Karkardooma courts, Delhi. dishonored due to insufficient funds, could have been issued in the course of this dispute, rather than for the repayment of a personal loan. The accused's defense, therefore, successfully rebuts the presumption under 140 Section 139 of the NI Act. He has provided a coherent narrative supported by relevant documents, demonstrating that the cheque was issued for business purposes and not to discharge a personal debt. Absence of Evidence by the Complainant In contrast to the accused's defense, the complainant has failed to provide 145 convincing evidence of the existence of a loan. The complainant claims that he lent ₹10,00,000/­ to the accused in May 2016, but this claim is unsupported by any documentary evidence such as a written agreement, promissory note, or bank transaction record. The absence of such evidence is a significant shortcoming in the complainant's case. 150 • Lack of Written Documentation: The complainant asserts that the loan was provided in cash, but there is no proof of this transaction. Cash loans, especially substantial amounts such as ₹10,00,000/­, are typically accompanied by some form of written agreement or acknowledgment to safeguard both parties' interests. The complainant's failure to produce such 155 documentation raises serious doubts about the authenticity of the loan transaction. • Failure to Provide Independent Evidence: The complainant did not CC no. 4816/2018 S. Dhanasekaran Vs. Selvaraj D. Page no. 8 / 11 In the court of Sh. Divyam Lila, MM, East district, Karkardooma courts, Delhi. produce any independent witnesses or corroborative evidence to support his claim that the loan was provided to the accused. Even if the loan was a 160 personal transaction, there should have been some form of documentation or at least the testimony of a third party to confirm the loan. The complainant did not produce his mother who had allegedly given the cash to the accused and had also allegedly accepted the cheque from the accused.The prime witness was not called to the court when the accused had clearly denied that 165 the cheque was issued by him for payment of any personal loan and also denied that he had actually taken the loan. • Lack of Bank Statements or Transfer Records: Given the size of the alleged loan, one would reasonably expect a transaction record, such as a bank transfer or deposit slip. The complainant has not provided any bank 170 records to show that ₹10,00,000/­ was transferred to the accused's account, nor has he shown any withdrawal of such a large sum from his own account to lend to the accused. This lack of documentary evidence severely weakens the complainant's case. The presumption under Section 139 of the NI Act cannot automatically be sustained 175 without the complainant presenting some form of tangible evidence of the debt. In this case, the complainant has failed to discharge his burden of proof to establish the existence of the loan and the debt that was allegedly repaid by the cheque. CC no. 4816/2018 S. Dhanasekaran Vs. Selvaraj D. Page no. 9 / 11 In the court of Sh. Divyam Lila, MM, East district, Karkardooma courts, Delhi. 10 Evaluation of the Preponderance of Probabilities 180 The standard of proof in criminal cases is "beyond a reasonable doubt," but in cases under Section 138 of the NI Act, the burden of proof is governed by the principle of preponderance of probabilities. The complainant must establish the existence of a debt or liability on the balance of probabilities, and the accused can rebut this by leading evidence to the contrary. 185 In this case, while the complainant has succeeded in proving the dishonor of the cheque, the accused has presented sufficient evidence to cast doubt on the complainant's claim. The accused has shown that the cheque was issued in connection with a business dispute, supported by documents showing ongoing litigation with the complainant's father. This evidence, when considered in 190 conjunction with the complainant's lack of documentary evidence regarding the loan, tips the balance of probabilities in favor of the accused. Given that the complainant has failed to prove the existence of the loan and the debt on a preponderance of probabilities, and considering the accused's rebuttal of the statutory presumption with credible evidence of a business relationship and 195 disputes, the complainant's case must fail. Conclusion The accused, Selvaraj, has successfully rebutted the presumption under Section 139 of the NI Act by providing a plausible and evidence­backed defense. The CC no. 4816/2018 S. Dhanasekaran Vs. Selvaraj D. Page no. 10 / 11 In the court of Sh. Divyam Lila, MM, East district, Karkardooma courts, Delhi. complainant has failed to prove the existence of a legally enforceable debt, as he 200 has not presented any documentary evidence to substantiate his claim of having lent ₹10,00,000/­ to the accused. Therefore, the complaint lacks merit. The court finds in favor of the accused Selvaraj D.. Therefore, the accused is found guilty under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881.
